text:
Recent work offers complementary diagnostic ideas. [ExUA (SIGIR 2024)](https://www.amazon.science/publications/explainable-uncertainty-attribution-for-sequential-recommendation) attributes recommendation uncertainty to individual historical interactions using gradient saliency. [CoDeR (AAAI 2025)](https://ojs.aaai.org/index.php/AAAI/article/view/33379) explicitly addresses demand shifts obscured by noise and bias. These motivate separating recent repeated support from isolated older evidence, without assuming either necessarily represents current demand.

[PROVE-REC (October 2026 preprint)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02968) links preference claims to selected history entries and tests both grounding and ranking influence: mask supporting evidence versus comparable control entries; remove claims and measure ranking-margin changes. Its use of reviews exceeds this task’s available evidence, but the verification principle transfers. Proposed adaptation: attach each diagnostic claim to training-history item IDs, timestamps, and exact title/description spans; record support frequency, recency, and specificity. Compare rank changes after removing recent repeated support versus isolated historical support, matching removal counts and checking position effects. These perturbations measure model dependence, not causal user preference.

[Know Your Limits (TACL 2025)](https://aclanthology.org/2025.tacl-1.26/) surveys abstention methods and evaluation. Practical adaptation: distinguish observed textual overlap, inferred interest, and unknown suitability; abstain when available evidence cannot establish fit. Report evidence coverage, unsupported-claim rate, abstention rate, and ranking sensitivity alongside fixed validation HR@10. Title/description similarity supports a relevance hypothesis; it cannot establish compatibility, ownership, present need, or satisfaction. Keep these as probes of the single trained NextItNet model, without adding independently fitted scoring components.
